rows.question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?

Under the Annex I route in Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Medical devices are Annex I harmonisation legislation, and the operator's device undergoes a third-party (notified-body) conformity assessment, so both conditions are met and the AI system is high-risk regardless of whether the device itself is labelled low, medium, or high risk. rows.pred_answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.
rows.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
rows.gold_answer: Both. The EU AI Act applies to AI systems and, through Chapter V, to general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. Article 2(1) sets the scope over AI systems placed on the market, put into service or used in the Union, and Article 2(12) extends that scope to GPAI models, so a model is regulated in its own right even before it is integrated into a system. "AI system" is defined in Article 3(1) and "general-purpose AI model" in Article 3(63); the two tracks differ in their obligations — high-risk AI systems carry the Chapter III Section 2 duties (Articles 9-15), while GPAI model providers carry the Chapter V duties (Article 53 documentation, copyright and training-data summary), with the Article 55 systemic-risk obligations where the Article 51 threshold (cumulative training compute above 10^25 FLOPs) is met.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.gold_answer: Not high-risk and not prohibited. Biometric verification used solely to confirm that a natural person is who he or she claims to be is expressly carved out of the high-risk biometrics category in Annex III, which limits that category to remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation, and emotion recognition, not one-to-one authentication of a claimed identity. It is likewise not among the exhaustively-listed practices banned under Article 5, none of which (subliminal or manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, and the other enumerated bans) captures identity verification. Absent the Annex III route, the system would be high-risk under Article 6 only where it functions as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment; failing that condition it falls outside the high-risk tier and is subject principally to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with natural persons.

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?

rows.question: What documentation does a provider of a high-risk AI system needs to keep available for the national competent authorities, and for how long?
rows.gold_answer: A provider of a high-risk AI system must keep, for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service, the documentation set out in Article 18 and make it available to national competent authorities on request. The declaration of conformity itself must likewise be kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years under Article 47.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.gold_answer: Article 14 governs human oversight. It requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use, through appropriate human-machine interface tools.
